newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's ruling Gaullists reject election reform.
newsitem.headline: France's ruling Gaullists reject election reform.

text.p: France's ruling Gaullist party on Wednesday rejected proposals to reform the voting system before a general election in 1998, a suggestion floated by its leader, Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

The executive of the RPR party believed that reforming the voting system ahead of the election could convey the impression that the Gaullists were worried about their prospects in the poll, RPR Secretary-General Jean-Francois Mancel told reporters.
Juppe suggested last month adding a "dose" of proportional representation to the majority voting system for parliamentary elections.

Such a reform would open the doors of the National Assembly to the far-right National Front which has been kept out of parliament by the first-past-the-post system. Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen won 15 percent of the vote in last year's presidential election.
In a related development, the opposition Socialist Party rebuffed wider proposals for electoral reform from Juppe.

Juppe had written to the leaders of all parliamentary parties this week asking their views on the voting system, the place of women and young people in politics, and the possibility of setting age limits for office-holders and limiting the number of posts a politician may hold at once.
In a reply released on Wednesday, Socialist leader Lionel Jospin sent Juppe his party's published proposals for limiting office-holding and increasing women's political role.

"On changing the voting system -- if that is your intention -- I do not believe this question is at the heart of the French people's expectations today, since they are much more concerned with economic difficulties and rising unemployment," he wrote.

The Paris daily Liberation said that, in his letter, Juppe had also raised the idea of barring triangular run-offs in parliamentary elections by limiting the second round to the top two candidates, where no one wins an outright majority on the first ballot.
That would hit the National Front which has vowed to keep its candidates in the race wherever it receives more than the required 12.5 percent of registered voters.
Jospin complained at being sent a multiple-choice questionnaire by Juppe.

"May I hope you share my view that asking us to fill in a questionnaire is neither a normal nor a fortunate formula for conducting relations between the prime minister and political leaders, especially with the opposition," he said.

Jospin noted that he had made modernising France's political institutions a major plank of his presidential election campaign 18 months ago, suggesting that the president's term of office be cut to five years from seven.
Conservative Gaullist President Jacques Chirac, who defeated Jospin, said at the time that constitutional reform was not the issue of the moment.
